{"id": "40:49/q12", "question": "What reduction of punishment do they seek?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:49/q12/p1", "position": "They ask for only a limited easing of punishment, not its permanent removal.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī says takhfīf means reducing punishment. Al-Samīn reads the partitive min as some punishment, for some day rather than all punishment on every day. Al-Biqāʿī and Bursawī say only part is to be relieved; Bursawī says a slight, short request reflects their knowledge that greater relief is impossible. Ibn ʿĀshūr says a day of respite would help more than merely reducing the fire’s intensity."}]}
{"id": "40:49/q13", "question": "What duration does يَوْمًۭا describe?", "turns_on": "Whether the measure is a worldly day or a figurative amount understood in the hereafter.", "positions": [{"id": "40:49/q13/p1", "position": "A measure equal to one day of this world.", "reasons": "Muqātil understands an omitted phrase, one day from the days of this world. Al-Ṭabarī says the afterlife has no night by which to measure a day and mentions 2:96. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursawī, and al-Ālūsī likewise give a worldly day’s measure."}, {"id": "40:49/q13/p2", "position": "A short amount of time or portion of punishment, rather than a literal measured day.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī allows an amount of time; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls day figurative for a little time and treats min al-ʿadhāb as explaining that amount. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī understands a portion of punishment, with day reckoned according to the nature of their realm."}]}
{"id": "40:49/q14", "question": "How do يَوْمًۭا and مِّنَ ٱلْعَذَابِ attach to يُخَفِّفْ?", "turns_on": "Whether day marks duration or is the object, and whether min is partitive, explanatory, or extra.", "positions": [{"id": "40:49/q14/p1", "position": "Day is an adverb of duration and min al-ʿadhāb is the partitive object of the verb.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn prefers this apparent parse: some of the punishment is eased for some day, without specifying one day or all days. Al-Ālūsī allows partitive min; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the phrase may attach directly to the verb."}, {"id": "40:49/q14/p2", "position": "Day is an adverb, while the object of the verb is omitted and min al-ʿadhāb explains or supplies it.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this parse and al-Akhfash’s view that min is extra, making al-ʿadhāb the object. Bursawī makes min al-ʿadhāb clarify the omitted object; al-Ālūsī gives the explanatory reading of min."}, {"id": "40:49/q14/p3", "position": "Day is the direct object, meaning a day’s punishment or its amount, with an omitted noun or explanatory min al-ʿadhāb.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī gives an omitted genitive as an alternative. Al-Samīn reports this parse but calls it strained with min al-ʿadhāb, and an emphatic-adjective treatment even weaker. Al-Ālūsī explains an omitted noun such as the torment of a day. Ibn ʿĀshūr says yukhafif can mean diminish and govern day directly, or an omitted ʿadhāb may supply its object."}]}
{"id": "40:49/q15", "question": "How do the keepers answer the plea?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:49/q15/p1", "position": "They refuse to pray for the inmates and tell them to pray for themselves.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī says the keepers will not pray for them. Abū Ḥayyān takes their reply as either mockery or a challenge, since they dare not make the request. Al-Qurazī’s report has the keepers recall that messengers brought clear proofs and then tell the inmates to pray; Abū al-Dardāʾ’s report also ends with the angels directing prayer and its futility."}]}
{"id": "40:49/q16", "question": "What sequence of events do reports add around this plea?", "turns_on": "The reports supply different preceding details and different wording of the keepers’ reply.", "positions": [{"id": "40:49/q16/p1", "position": "Hunger, painful food and scalding drink precede the appeal to the angels, who tell the inmates to pray to no avail.", "reasons": "Abū al-Dardāʾ’s report, cited by al-Naḥḥās and by al-Qurṭubī from al-Tirmidhī and others, describes hunger, unsatisfying thorny and choking food, and boiling drink that scalds faces and cuts bowels before the plea. The two notes vary in detail, but recount the same sequence."}, {"id": "40:49/q16/p2", "position": "The inmates beg for a day’s relief, and the keepers recall the messengers’ proofs before directing them to pray.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports al-Qurazī as saying he was told this sequence, including that unbelievers’ prayers prove futile."}]}
{"id": "40:49/q17", "question": "Can the inmates’ prayer or repentance now avert punishment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:49/q17/p1", "position": "Their late pleas cannot avert or alleviate the punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī says the disbelievers’ prayer is futile. Al-Ṭabrisī says they know necessarily that punishment never ends or lessens but still hope for relief. Study Quran says belated affirmation and supplication are too late, citing 14:44, 32:12 and 6:27; even a return would lead them to repeat forbidden conduct (6:28). Kuranyolu says after judgment no one can rescue another and even angels refuse."}]}
{"id": "40:49/q18", "question": "How does this appeal relate to the preceding exchange between followers and leaders?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:49/q18/p1", "position": "After leaders prove unable to relieve their followers, both groups are in the Fire and turn to the keepers.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī, Bursawī, and al-Ālūsī include followers and leaders, weak and arrogant, among the petitioners. Kuranyolu, citing Rāzī, says those who followed powerful deniers had asked their leaders to remove even part of the fire; the leaders could save nobody, and the followers may have known this, exposing their helplessness. Study Quran likewise says worldly protectors cannot help them (6:27–28; 14:44)."}]}
{"id": "40:49/q19", "question": "What practical warning does this scene convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:49/q19/p1", "position": "Seek salvation before Judgment by rejecting dominant misleaders and following the messenger’s clear guidance.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says people should freely choose belief and conduct rather than follow wealthy, influential immoral deniers; after judgment no one can save another except by God’s will, even angels refuse pleas. It urges resistance to inner desires and dominant misleaders in this life and adherence to the messenger’s pure way."}]}
{"id": "40:49/q20", "question": "How does this scene fit the sūra’s warning and Moses–Pharaoh narrative?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:49/q20/p1", "position": "The judgment scene extends the warning that rejecting God’s messenger ends in ruin despite worldly power, while the Moses–Pharaoh narrative encourages steadfastness.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says Moses and Pharaoh’s story supports the earlier claim about destroyed rejecters, warns Quraysh, and urges Muhammad and his companions to endure until victory; the believer in Pharaoh’s family is a lesson for hesitant sympathizers. Study Quran says the Hereafter warning in verses 10–20 prepares the extended narrative centered on that believer (40:28, 40:45)."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q01", "question": "Who speaks in this exchange, and whom do they address?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q01/p1", "position": "The keepers of Hell address its condemned inhabitants, who answer them.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies the messengers as coming from the inmates' own people. Al-Kashshāf identifies the keepers as attendants charged with torment. Ibn ʿĀshūr argues that the plural messengers and mention of guardians point to Hell's people generally, rather than only Pharaoh's family, who had Moses alone."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q02", "question": "When do the keepers reply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q02/p1", "position": "They answer after a delay.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī calls it a long interval; Bursevī likewise notes a delayed answer."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q03", "question": "How does the opening أَوَلَمْ attach to the preceding speech?", "turns_on": "Which implicit response supplies the coordinate of the waw.", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q03/p1", "position": "The interrogative hamza introduces a question whose waw coordinates it with an understood prior thought: 'Did you not take notice of this?'", "reasons": "Bursevī supplies the omitted sense and identifies the hamza as interrogative."}, {"id": "40:50/q03/p2", "position": "The waw joins the keepers' words to the inmates' request by prompting the reply the inmates ought to have given.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this ʿaṭf al-talqīn and compares 2:124."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q04", "question": "Why do the keepers ask whether messengers brought proofs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q04/p1", "position": "They compel an admission of established guidance and rebuke the inmates for rejecting it and wasting the time when prayer could help.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says the question forces proof and recalls neglected conditions of answered prayer. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Nasafī call it rebuke; al-Bayḍāwī adds admission of evidence. Al-Ṭabrisī says they stubbornly resisted proofs of unity and prophethood. Al-Biqāʿī says the question exposes why they are unworthy of a hearing: they failed to use reason. Bursevī and al-Ālūsī say the proofs warned of the evil end of disbelief and sins and established guilt; al-Ālūsī compares 39:71. Ibn ʿĀshūr says it recalls everlasting punishment and their blameworthy choice. The Study Quran compares 6:130, 39:71, and 67:8–9."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q05", "question": "What is the implicit subject of تَكُ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q05/p1", "position": "The omitted subject of kāna is the story or occasion, explained by the following clause about messengers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī supplies al-qiṣṣa; al-Nasafī says the story or occasion."}]}

{"id": "40:50/q07", "question": "What is conveyed by the omitted nūn of تَكُ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q07/p1", "position": "It evokes the messengers' gradual ascent from immediate sensory proofs to reason, remembrance, and certainty.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī gives this explanation in al-Burhān; al-Sāmarrāʾī reports it, saying the movement is from ignorance through accessible sensory signs to certainty. {"id": "40:50/q08", "question": "What does the form تَأْتِيكُمْ suggest about the messengers' coming?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q08/p1", "position": "Their coming in worldly life was repeated or continuous.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī attributes successive coming to the imperfect tense and also notes the omitted nūn of تك. {"id": "40:50/q09", "question": "What is the force of رُسُلُكُم, 'your messengers'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q09/p1", "position": "The messengers were human beings from among the addressed people's own kind, which gave them reason to listen.", "reasons": "Muqātil says they came from among the people themselves. Al-Biqāʿī says people are more receptive to those of their own kind."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q10", "question": "How is the sīn of رُسُلُكُم read?", "turns_on": "The competing transmissions for Abū ʿAmr and the usual reading of the other readers.", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q10/p1", "position": "It is lightened with sukūn, yielding ruslukum.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid reports Abū ʿAmr's lightening in plurals attached to a two-letter pronoun, with parallels رسلنا and رسلك; one report attributes the light reading of رسلك to him. Qiraat-Er says this compresses the sound without changing referent or syntax."}, {"id": "40:50/q10/p2", "position": "It is read heavy, with the sīn vocalized.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid reports another transmission from Abū ʿAmr reading رسلك heavily, as the other readers generally do."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q11", "question": "What are the بَيِّنَٰت brought by the messengers?", "turns_on": "Which content of the messengers' clear evidence is being specified; the notes give compatible specifications rather than a stated polemic.", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q11/p1", "position": "Clear signs warning of the evil end of disbelief and sin.", "reasons": "Bursevī says these warnings establish guilt; al-Ālūsī says the messengers repeatedly brought them in worldly life and compares 39:71."}, {"id": "40:50/q11/p2", "position": "Unmistakable proofs together with explicit calls to follow guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr includes the explicit calls. Al-Biqāʿī describes the proofs as clearer than anything else."}, {"id": "40:50/q11/p3", "position": "Miracles.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī gives this gloss."}, {"id": "40:50/q11/p4", "position": "Clear proofs of God's unity and the messengers' prophethood.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī specifies both matters against which the sinners resisted."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q12", "question": "What do the inmates acknowledge by answering بَلَىٰ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q12/p1", "position": "They concede that messengers and their proofs came, despite their own rejection of the messengers.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī adds that they denied the messengers' prophethood. Bursevī and al-Ālūsī compare the explicit confession in Sūrat al-Mulk, 67:9. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the bayyināt proofs and calls to guidance. Al-Nasafī says the admission precedes the keepers' mockery."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q13", "question": "Where may one stop at بَلَىٰ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q13/p1", "position": "Stopping at بلى is preferred because it completes the answer without syntactic dependence on what follows; some also allow beginning there.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī reports this preference of many readers and linguists for ten occurrences."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q14", "question": "How does the fa in فَٱدْعُوا۟ follow the admission?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q14/p1", "position": "It makes the order to pray a consequence of their admission that they rejected the messengers' proofs.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls the fa explanatory with an ellipsis: since they admit it, they must pray themselves. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the sequence follows naturally under either analysis of the preceding waw."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q15", "question": "What do the keepers mean by فَٱدْعُوا۟?", "turns_on": "Whether the imperative directs them to pray for themselves, exposes their former false objects, invites a curse, or dismisses prayer entirely.", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q15/p1", "position": "Pray for yourselves: the keepers decline to intercede, and the instruction rebukes or mocks the inmates without promising an answer.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr, and classical commentators reported by Asad explain the refusal to pray for them. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Nasafī call the command mocking; al-Ṭabrisī reports contemptuous dismissal. Al-Kashshāf, Bursevī, al-Ālūsī, and al-Bayḍāwī stress despair rather than hope; al-Kashshāf reasons that if a close angel's prayer is unheard, theirs will be worse. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it permission or equal treatment and cites the saying that one who chooses its cool must bear its heat. Al-Biqāʿī allows prayer now to God, human messengers, angels, or others; Muqātil and Ibn Kathīr say it changes nothing."}, {"id": "40:50/q15/p2", "position": "Invoke the false objects and values once treated as divine, to see whether they can help.", "reasons": "Asad prefers this reading and cites the next clause: those prayers were deluded in earthly life, whereas the delusions are gone on Judgment Day."}, {"id": "40:50/q15/p3", "position": "Pray for woe and destruction.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī reports this alternative."}, {"id": "40:50/q15/p4", "position": "Stop praying, because no one will hear you.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī gives this as an alternative to the command to pray now."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q16", "question": "Why do the keepers refuse to pray for the inmates?", "turns_on": "Whether refusal is explained by the inmates' conduct, lack of divine permission, or the settled impossibility of relief.", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q16/p1", "position": "The inmates' own rejection of guidance makes them unworthy of intercession.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the fa grounds the refusal in their conduct and rejects a bare lack-of-permission explanation for missing this connection. Ibn ʿĀshūr says they chose to turn away from the messengers and are left to manage their own affairs. Bursevī calls it implausible that the keepers would pray for them."}, {"id": "40:50/q16/p2", "position": "The keepers have no permission to intercede for such sinners.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says angels can intercede only for a nonevildoer, with permission, before final judgment; al-Ṭabrisī says the guards have not received permission; al-Bayḍāwī says they dare not pray without it. Al-Ālūsī rejects this explanation because it fails to account for the fa and implies that a change in permission could have changed their case."}, {"id": "40:50/q16/p3", "position": "They know the punishment will not be reduced and their prayer cannot bring release.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī explicitly gives the impossibility of reduction. Ibn Kathīr says they refuse help or a request for release because prayer will change nothing. Al-Wāḥidī describes their refusal; the Study Quran says even belated affirmation cannot avert or alleviate punishment and compares 14:44, 32:12, and 6:27."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q17", "question": "Who says the closing statement about futile prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the closing clause continues the dialogue or is a divine aside; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes a parenthetic waw for the latter.", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q17/p1", "position": "The keepers continue speaking to the inmates.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this view. Abū Ḥayyān calls it the apparent reading; al-Nasafī calls it a continuation of their taunt. Al-Ālūsī attributes the sentence to the keepers. Ibn ʿĀshūr allows it as their concluding warning."}, {"id": "40:50/q17/p2", "position": "God reports the conclusion to Muhammad as a parenthetical statement.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Ālūsī report this alternative. Ibn ʿĀshūr permits it and takes the waw as parenthetic."}]}

{"id": "40:50/q22", "question": "What does it mean that disbelievers' prayer is فِى ضَلَٰلٍ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q22/p1", "position": "Their pleas bring no benefit, acceptance, answer, or relief from punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Nasafī call the prayer fruitless; al-Bayḍāwī says the clause extinguishes hope. Al-Biqāʿī compares the futility of their worldly deeds: the Hereafter harvests what this life plants. Bursevī says the prayer is made at the wrong time. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the denial generic across times and places, whether spoken by angels or God. The Study Quran says belated affirmation cannot alleviate punishment, with parallel pleas at 14:44, 32:12, and 6:27."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q23", "question": "Which prayers does the closing statement have in view?", "turns_on": "Whether the generic wording applies to the present afterlife plea, every disbeliever's prayer, or their former idolatrous invocations.", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q23/p1", "position": "The condemned people's pleas on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Bursevī says they pray at the wrong time. Al-Ālūsī expressly limits the verse's denial to their prayer on Judgment Day, while allowing worldly requests to be granted. Al-Bayḍāwī and the Study Quran connect it to despair of relief from the present punishment."}, {"id": "40:50/q23/p2", "position": "Disbelievers' prayers generally, across times and places.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr argues that the generic annexed noun gives universal scope, regardless of speaker. Al-Ālūsī restricts this inference to Judgment Day."}, {"id": "40:50/q23/p3", "position": "Invocations directed to idols or false objects in worldly life, which prove deluded or unanswered.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī says idols cannot answer anyone in this life or the next; Qatāda says idols have no answered prayer. Asad says earthly delusions have vanished by Judgment Day. Bursevī cites Saʿdī's poem: an idol fails its devotee for years, but God grants the need when the desperate man collapses at the temple."}]}
{"id": "40:50/q24", "question": "Can a disbeliever's worldly prayer be answered?", "turns_on": "Whether a worldly grant counts as an answered prayer and whether the verse's denial extends beyond Judgment Day.", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q24/p1", "position": "It is not accepted as an answered prayer, even if a requested rescue occurs.", "reasons": "The majority reported by Bursevī cite this verse, arguing that disbelief entails not knowing God or invalidating belief by describing Him wrongly. Ibn ʿĀshūr says rescues in 6:63–64 and 10:22–23 expose ingratitude, not honorable acceptance; a rescue may have been decreed already or coincide with righteous people's prayers. He cites the Muslim report from Abū Hurayra in which the Prophet questions how a traveler nourished by unlawful food and drink could have his raised-hands prayer answered."}, {"id": "40:50/q24/p2", "position": "A wronged disbeliever's prayer can be answered.", "reasons": "Some reported by Bursevī interpret kufr here as ingratitude and cite God's granting Satan's request for respite. Bursevī says this permissive ruling is followed and himself adduces Satan's granted request."}, {"id": "40:50/q24/p3", "position": "Worldly requests may be granted; this verse only settles the fate of prayers on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says some infer from the verse that no disbeliever's prayer is answered and that disbelievers cannot join the rain prayer, but he limits its scope to the Day of Judgment and leaves open what one calls a worldly grant."}]}

{"id": "40:50/q26", "question": "Why did the condemned turn to the keepers for help?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "40:50/q26/p1", "position": "They sought someone who might intercede or lessen the fire, though no creature could free them.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf suggests the worst rebels are in this fire and deliberately approach assigned angels, whose closeness to God might make their prayers more likely to be heard. Al-Kashshāf identifies the keepers as attendants charged with torment."}]}
